subject: Culture
title: Eating Insects
description: A short lesson to help you apply Eating Insects.

hook.text: Two billion people already eat insects. The West treats it as a dare.

buildup.text: Crickets have more protein per pound than beef and need a fraction of the water and land.

discovery.text: In Thailand, fried crickets are a beloved snack. In Mexico, chapulines top tacos. It's normal food.

twist.text: Western disgust at insects is the outlier, not the norm. Entomophagy is the human default.

climax.text: The barrier to eating insects isn't nutrition or taste. It's culture—and culture can change.

punchline.text: The future protein might already be crawling.

quiz.question: Approximately how many people worldwide already eat insects?

details.summary: Over two billion people worldwide eat insects regularly — crickets, ants, beetles, and caterpillars are protein-rich staples in much of Asia, Africa, and Latin America. The Western taboo against entomophagy is the global exception, not the rule, and it may be an obstacle to sustainable food futures.
details.whyItMatters: Insect eating could help solve global food security and environmental challenges. Overcoming the Western disgust response may be necessary for sustainable protein production.
takeaways: Over 2,000 insect species are eaten worldwide
Insects produce 80% less methane than cattle per gram of protein
The Western insect taboo is culturally learned, not biological

faq.question: Why don't Western cultures eat insects?
faq.answer: Temperate climates produce fewer large, easily harvested edible insects than tropical regions. As European agriculture focused on livestock, insects became associated with contamination and poverty.

faq.question: Are insects really more sustainable than meat?
faq.answer: Dramatically so. Crickets require 12 times less feed, 2,000 times less water, and produce 100 times less greenhouse gas than beef per kilogram of protein. They can be raised on food waste in small spaces.
